questiontext.text: An Extended Finite-State Machine (EFSM) differs from a plain FSM chiefly by adding what?

answer.text: Data (context) variables, with transitions carrying guard conditions over those variables

feedback.text: Correct — an EFSM extends a plain FSM with data variables and guards (and possibly updates) over them.

answer.text: More states, but still no conditions on any transition

feedback.text: Adding states does not make a machine "extended"; the extension is data variables plus guards.

answer.text: A requirement that every transition be a self-loop

feedback.text: Self-loops are unrelated; the EFSM extension is data variables and guarded transitions.

answer.text: The removal of the initial state

feedback.text: An EFSM still has an initial state; what it adds is data variables and guards.

generalfeedback.text: A plain FSM has only states and events. An EFSM extends it with data (context) variables; transitions carry guard conditions over those variables and may update them. The app's model uses one variable, amount, with guards such as amount <= 100.

questiontext.text: In this EFSM, what is a guard on a transition?

answer.text: A boolean condition over the data variable that must hold for the transition to fire

feedback.text: Correct — e.g. amount <= 100 must be true for the approve transition to fire.

answer.text: The event name that triggers the transition

feedback.text: That is the event (e.g. approve); the guard is the extra condition on it.

answer.text: The destination state of the transition

feedback.text: The destination is where the transition leads; the guard decides whether it may fire.

answer.text: The concrete input value chosen by the solver

feedback.text: The solver picks a value that satisfies the guards; the guard itself is the condition.

generalfeedback.text: A guard is a boolean condition over the context variable (here amount). When its event occurs, the transition fires only if the guard evaluates to true — for example approve fires only when amount <= 100.

questiontext.text: What is a context (data) variable in an EFSM?

answer.text: A variable the machine carries whose value the guards test to decide which transitions may fire

feedback.text: Correct — here amount is the context variable that every guard is written over.

answer.text: A synonym for the current state

feedback.text: The state is the mode the machine is in; a context variable is separate data the guards read.

answer.text: The list of events the machine accepts

feedback.text: Those are events; a context variable is data whose value guards evaluate.

answer.text: The name of a transition

feedback.text: Transitions are identified by their event and endpoints; a context variable holds data.

generalfeedback.text: A context (data) variable is state carried alongside the control state; guards are predicates over it. This model has exactly one such variable, amount (an integer input).

questiontext.text: In an EFSM, a transition is enabled when...

answer.text: its event occurs in the current state and its guard evaluates to true

feedback.text: Correct — both the event and a satisfied guard are needed for the transition to fire.

answer.text: its event occurs, regardless of the guard

feedback.text: Even if the event occurs, a false guard blocks the transition; it is not enabled.

answer.text: its guard is true, regardless of which event occurs

feedback.text: A true guard alone is not enough; the matching event must also occur.

answer.text: the machine is in its initial state

feedback.text: Being in the initial state does not by itself enable any particular transition.

generalfeedback.text: A transition is enabled (may fire) only when both conditions hold: its triggering event occurs in the current state, and its guard evaluates to true for the current variable value.

questiontext.text: In the general EFSM model, what is an update (or action) on a transition?

answer.text: An assignment that changes a data variable's value when the transition fires

feedback.text: Correct — updates modify context variables (this app's model happens to use guards only, with no updates).

answer.text: The boolean condition checked before firing

feedback.text: That is the guard, not the update; an update changes a variable's value.

answer.text: The event that triggers the transition

feedback.text: The event is the trigger; the update is the effect on the data.

answer.text: The destination state

feedback.text: The destination is control flow; an update is the data assignment performed while firing.

generalfeedback.text: In a full EFSM a transition can both test variables (guard) and change them (update/action), e.g. attempts := attempts + 1. This app's withdrawal model uses guards over the input amount only and performs no updates, so amount keeps its input value along a path.

questiontext.text: In the app's withdrawal-request EFSM, what is the single data variable that all guards are written over?

answer.text: amount, an integer input

feedback.text: Correct — the model has one variable, amount, and every guard tests it.

answer.text: balance

feedback.text: There is no balance variable in this model; the only variable is amount.

answer.text: attempts

feedback.text: attempts belongs to a different example; this model's variable is amount.

answer.text: state

feedback.text: state is the control mode, not the data variable; the data variable is amount.

generalfeedback.text: The model declares one variable: amount (an integer input). The daily limit (100) and fraud threshold (200) are not variables — they appear as constants inside the guards.

questiontext.text: In the model, the daily withdrawal limit appears as which constant inside the guards?

answer.text: 100 — in the guards amount <= 100 (approve) and amount >= 101 (decline)

feedback.text: Correct — the daily limit 100 splits Checking into approve (<= 100) and decline (>= 101).
200 is the fraud threshold (guard amount >= 200 on fraudHold), not the daily limit.
50 is the recheck guard constant (amount <= 50), not the daily limit.
1 is the enterAmount guard constant (amount >= 1), not the daily limit.

generalfeedback.text: The daily limit is encoded as 100: approve requires amount <= 100 and decline requires amount >= 101. The fraud threshold (200) is a separate constant on fraudHold.

questiontext.text: Which transition carries the guard amount >= 200, encoding the fraud threshold?

answer.text: fraudHold, from Approved to Denied

feedback.text: Correct — fraudHold fires from Approved to Denied only when amount >= 200.

answer.text: approve, from Checking to Approved

feedback.text: approve's guard is amount <= 100, not amount >= 200.

answer.text: decline, from Checking to Denied

feedback.text: decline's guard is amount >= 101, not amount >= 200.

answer.text: enterAmount, from Idle to Checking

feedback.text: enterAmount's guard is amount >= 1, not amount >= 200.

generalfeedback.text: The fraud threshold 200 appears on fraudHold: Approved --fraudHold [amount >= 200]--> Denied. It flags an already-approved request as fraudulent when the amount is large.

questiontext.text: What guard does the enterAmount transition (Idle to Checking) carry?

answer.text: amount >= 1

feedback.text: Correct — you can only enter Checking with a positive amount.

answer.text: amount <= 100

feedback.text: That is the approve guard, not enterAmount.

answer.text: amount >= 200

feedback.text: That is the fraudHold guard, not enterAmount.

answer.text: no guard (always true)

feedback.text: enterAmount does have a guard, amount >= 1; dispense and eject are the unguarded transitions.

generalfeedback.text: enterAmount fires from Idle to Checking under the guard amount >= 1, so a non-positive amount cannot start a check.

questiontext.text: What guard does the approve transition (Checking to Approved) carry?

answer.text: amount <= 100

feedback.text: Correct — approve fires only when the amount is within the daily limit.

answer.text: amount >= 101

feedback.text: That is the decline guard, the complementary branch out of Checking.

answer.text: amount <= 50

feedback.text: That is the recheck guard (Approved to Checking), not approve.

answer.text: amount >= 1

feedback.text: That is the enterAmount guard, not approve.

generalfeedback.text: approve fires from Checking to Approved under amount <= 100. Its complement, decline (amount >= 101), leaves Checking for Denied.

questiontext.text: Which transitions in the model have no guard (shown as a dash, guard = true)?

answer.text: dispense (Approved to Idle) and eject (Denied to Idle)

feedback.text: Correct — both are unconditional; they always fire when their event occurs.

answer.text: approve and decline

feedback.text: approve (amount <= 100) and decline (amount >= 101) are both guarded.

answer.text: enterAmount and recheck

feedback.text: enterAmount (amount >= 1) and recheck (amount <= 50) are both guarded.

answer.text: fraudHold and approve

feedback.text: fraudHold (amount >= 200) and approve (amount <= 100) are both guarded.

generalfeedback.text: Only dispense and eject carry guard = true (drawn as a dash). Both return the machine to Idle unconditionally once their event occurs.

questiontext.text: What is the initial state of the withdrawal-request EFSM?

answer.text: Idle

feedback.text: Correct — the machine starts in Idle and returns there via dispense or eject.

answer.text: Checking

feedback.text: Checking is reached after enterAmount; the machine starts in Idle.

answer.text: Approved

feedback.text: Approved is reached via approve; it is not the start state.

answer.text: Denied

feedback.text: Denied is reached via decline or fraudHold; it is not the start state.

generalfeedback.text: The model declares Idle as the initial state. Every abstract test path starts and ends at Idle.

name.text: Why guards split the Checking edge

questiontext.text: According to the app, what do the guards amount <= 100 and amount >= 101 do to the "leave Checking" edge?

answer.text: They split one edge into two mutually exclusive branches (approve and decline)

feedback.text: Correct — exactly one of the two guards can hold for any amount, so the branches are mutually exclusive.

answer.text: They make Checking unreachable

feedback.text: Checking is reachable via enterAmount; the guards only split its outgoing edge.

answer.text: They allow both approve and decline to fire at once

feedback.text: The guards are complementary, so at most one can hold; they are mutually exclusive.

answer.text: They delete the Checking state entirely

feedback.text: Checking stays; the guards partition how the machine leaves it.

generalfeedback.text: The daily-limit guards amount <= 100 and amount >= 101 partition every amount into exactly one branch: approve (within limit) or decline (over limit). One graph edge becomes two mutually exclusive guarded branches.

questiontext.text: In this explorer, what does it mean for an abstract path to be infeasible?

answer.text: No input value can satisfy all the path's guards at once — their conjunction is unsatisfiable

feedback.text: Correct — feasibility is satisfiability of the conjunction of the path's guards.

answer.text: The path visits a state that does not exist

feedback.text: Every path is graph-valid; infeasibility is about the guards, not missing states.

answer.text: The path is longer than the number of states

feedback.text: Length has nothing to do with feasibility; the guard conjunction is what matters.

answer.text: The path has no guards on any transition

feedback.text: A path with no guards is trivially feasible; infeasibility means the guards contradict.

generalfeedback.text: An abstract path is a graph-valid event sequence. It is infeasible when the conjunction of its transitions' guards has no solution — no single amount can make them all true — so no test can exercise it.

name.text: What the solver reports for a feasible path

questiontext.text: When a path is feasible, what does the explorer hand back?

answer.text: A concrete input value for amount that satisfies all the path's guards

feedback.text: Correct — feasible paths go to the constraint solver, which yields a witness value of amount.

answer.text: A proof that the path can never be executed

feedback.text: That would describe an infeasible path; a feasible path yields a concrete input.

answer.text: A new state added to the machine

feedback.text: The solver does not add states; it produces a concrete amount value.

answer.text: The number of events in the path

feedback.text: The solver returns a satisfying amount, not a count of events.

generalfeedback.text: Feasible paths are handed to the constraint solver, which returns a concrete witness value of amount that satisfies the whole guard conjunction — a ready-made test input.

answer.text: It prevents starting a check with a non-positive amount (amount <= 0 stays in Idle)

name.text: Satisfied guards in Approved at amount=250

answer.text: fraudHold and dispense

questiontext.text: Path PA is enterAmount · approve · dispense, collecting guards amount >= 1 and amount <= 100. The solver picks the smallest-magnitude integer that satisfies both. What value of amount does it report?

feedback.text: Correct — the feasible set is 1 to 100; the smallest-magnitude integer in it is 1.
0 fails amount >= 1, so it is not in the feasible set.
100 satisfies both guards but is not the smallest-magnitude solution; 1 is.
50 is a valid witness but not the smallest; the solver reports 1.

generalfeedback.text: PA's guard conjunction is amount >= 1 and amount <= 100, i.e. the interval [1, 100]. The solver returns the integer of smallest absolute value in that interval, which is 1.

questiontext.text: Path PB is enterAmount · decline · eject, collecting guards amount >= 1 and amount >= 101. What value of amount does the solver report (smallest-magnitude integer satisfying both)?

feedback.text: Correct — the two guards intersect to amount >= 101, whose smallest integer is 101.
1 satisfies amount >= 1 but not amount >= 101, so it is not feasible for PB.
100 fails amount >= 101; the smallest feasible integer is 101.
102 is feasible but not the smallest; 101 is the smallest integer with amount >= 101.

generalfeedback.text: amount >= 1 and amount >= 101 intersect to amount >= 101. The smallest-magnitude integer satisfying that is 101, so the solver reports amount = 101.

questiontext.text: Path PC is enterAmount · approve · fraudHold · eject, collecting guards amount >= 1, amount <= 100, and amount >= 200. Why is it infeasible?

answer.text: No amount can satisfy amount <= 100 and amount >= 200 at once — the conjunction is unsatisfiable

feedback.text: Correct — approve requires at most 100 while fraudHold requires at least 200, which cannot both hold.

answer.text: Because it passes through the Denied state

feedback.text: Visiting Denied is fine; the path is infeasible because two guards contradict.

answer.text: Because eject has no guard

feedback.text: An unguarded transition adds no constraint; infeasibility comes from amount <= 100 and amount >= 200.

answer.text: Because the path has four transitions

feedback.text: Length is irrelevant; the contradiction between amount <= 100 and amount >= 200 makes it infeasible.

generalfeedback.text: To take approve then fraudHold on the same input, amount must be both <= 100 and >= 200. No integer satisfies both, so the guard conjunction is unsatisfiable and PC is infeasible.

questiontext.text: Path PD is enterAmount · approve · recheck · decline · eject, collecting guards amount >= 1, amount <= 100, amount <= 50, and amount >= 101. Why is it infeasible?

answer.text: recheck requires amount <= 50 while decline requires amount >= 101, and no amount satisfies both

answer.text: Because it revisits the Checking state

feedback.text: Revisiting a state is allowed; the contradiction is between amount <= 50 and amount >= 101.

answer.text: Because it is the longest path in the model

feedback.text: Length does not decide feasibility; the guard conjunction being unsatisfiable does.

answer.text: Because approve and decline are the same event

feedback.text: approve and decline are distinct events; infeasibility is due to amount <= 50 versus amount >= 101.

generalfeedback.text: After recheck (amount <= 50) the path then needs decline (amount >= 101) on the same input amount. Since amount cannot be both at most 50 and at least 101, the conjunction has no solution and PD is infeasible.

questiontext.text: Path PE is enterAmount · approve · recheck · approve · dispense, collecting guards amount >= 1, amount <= 100, amount <= 50, and amount <= 100. Is it feasible, and what does the solver report?

answer.text: Feasible; the guards reduce to 1 <= amount <= 50, and the solver reports amount = 1

feedback.text: Correct — the two amount <= 100 clauses are subsumed by amount <= 50, leaving [1, 50]; the smallest integer is 1.

answer.text: Infeasible, because recheck and approve conflict

feedback.text: They do not conflict: amount <= 50 also satisfies amount <= 100, so the intersection [1, 50] is non-empty.

answer.text: Feasible; the solver reports amount = 50

feedback.text: 50 is a valid witness but not the smallest; the solver reports 1.

answer.text: Infeasible, because it takes approve twice

generalfeedback.text: PE's guards are amount >= 1, amount <= 100, amount <= 50, amount <= 100. The tightest bounds give 1 <= amount <= 50, which is satisfiable, so PE is feasible and the solver returns the smallest-magnitude integer, amount = 1.

name.text: Why one amount must satisfy all guards

answer.text: amount is an input set once and never updated, so the whole path runs on that one value and its guards conjunct

feedback.text: Correct — with no updates, the same amount is tested at every step, so all guards must hold together.

answer.text: Because each transition reassigns amount to a new value

feedback.text: This model has no updates; amount is not reassigned, which is exactly why one value must satisfy all guards.

answer.text: Because guards are evaluated only at the initial state

feedback.text: Each transition's guard is checked when that transition fires, but all on the same fixed amount.

answer.text: Because the solver can only try one number in total

feedback.text: The solver searches many values; the point is that one amount must satisfy the whole conjunction.

generalfeedback.text: In this model amount is a pure input with no update actions, so its value is fixed for the entire run. Feasibility therefore requires one amount to satisfy the conjunction of all the path's guards simultaneously.

name.text: Why EFSM needs guard-aware test generation

questiontext.text: Why is guard-aware test generation needed for an EFSM, rather than plain FSM graph-path coverage?

answer.text: Some graph-valid paths are infeasible; naive path coverage wastes effort chasing inputs that cannot exist

feedback.text: Correct — guards make certain abstract paths unexecutable, so tests must be derived with the guards in mind.

answer.text: EFSMs have no states, so ordinary coverage does not apply

feedback.text: EFSMs still have states; the issue is that guards render some paths infeasible.

answer.text: Guard-aware generation is only about making tests run faster

feedback.text: The point is correctness of the test targets, not speed: it avoids impossible paths.

answer.text: Because every EFSM path is always feasible

feedback.text: The opposite is true — some paths are infeasible, which is why guards must be considered.

generalfeedback.text: A graph-only view treats all 5 paths as test targets, but 2 are infeasible. Generating tests for them wastes effort searching for inputs that cannot exist. Guard-aware generation only targets paths whose guard conjunction is satisfiable.

questiontext.text: The comparison shows FSM (graph paths) = 5 and EFSM (feasible) = 3. What does the gap of 2 represent?

answer.text: The 2 abstract paths (PC and PD) that guards prune as infeasible

feedback.text: Correct — the gap is exactly the paths whose guard conjunction is unsatisfiable.

answer.text: The 2 states that the EFSM removed from the FSM

feedback.text: No states are removed; the gap counts pruned paths, not states.

answer.text: The 2 extra events the EFSM adds

feedback.text: No events are added; the gap is the infeasible paths dropped.

answer.text: The 2 guards that always evaluate to true

feedback.text: The gap is a count of pruned paths, not of unguarded transitions.

generalfeedback.text: The FSM bar counts all 5 graph paths; the EFSM bar counts the 3 feasible ones. The difference, 2, is the number of paths guards prune as infeasible (PC and PD) — tests that plain path coverage would have chased in vain.

questiontext.text: Could reordering the transitions of PC (which needs both amount <= 100 and amount >= 200) make it feasible?

answer.text: No — feasibility depends on the conjunction of guards, which is order-independent and still unsatisfiable

feedback.text: Correct — logical AND is commutative, so no ordering rescues an unsatisfiable conjunction.

answer.text: Yes — checking amount >= 200 before amount <= 100 would pass

feedback.text: Order does not matter for a conjunction; both must hold at once, which is impossible.

answer.text: Yes — as long as an unguarded transition comes last

feedback.text: An unguarded transition adds no constraint and cannot fix the contradiction.

answer.text: Only if amount is updated between the two guards

feedback.text: This model has no updates; and PC's infeasibility is inherent to requiring amount <= 100 and amount >= 200 together.

generalfeedback.text: Because amount is fixed and feasibility is the satisfiability of the AND of all guards, order is irrelevant. amount <= 100 and amount >= 200 have empty intersection under any ordering, so PC stays infeasible.

questiontext.text: Start in Idle with amount = 40 and fire, in order, enterAmount, approve, recheck, approve, dispense. Which abstract path is realized, and is 40 a valid witness?

answer.text: Path PE, and 40 is valid (all of amount >= 1, amount <= 100, amount <= 50 hold)

feedback.text: Correct — 40 satisfies every guard on PE, so the trace runs to completion and returns to Idle.

answer.text: Path PA, and 40 is valid

feedback.text: PA is enterAmount, approve, dispense; the given trace includes recheck and a second approve, which is PE.

answer.text: Path PE, but 40 is invalid because recheck needs amount <= 50

feedback.text: 40 <= 50 is true, so recheck's guard holds; 40 is a valid witness.

answer.text: Path PD, and 40 is valid

feedback.text: PD ends with decline to Denied; the given trace ends with a second approve and dispense, which is PE.

generalfeedback.text: enterAmount (40 >= 1), approve (40 <= 100), recheck (40 <= 50), approve (40 <= 100), dispense: this is exactly path PE, and 40 satisfies every guard, so it is a valid witness (though the solver's smallest is 1).

questiontext.text: Start in Idle with amount = 120. enterAmount fires (120 >= 1) to Checking. On the same input, which feasible path can the machine complete back to Idle?

answer.text: Path PB (enterAmount, decline, eject) — 120 fails approve (amount <= 100) but satisfies decline (amount >= 101)

feedback.text: Correct — at 120 the Checking split resolves to decline, leading to Denied then eject back to Idle.

answer.text: Path PA (enterAmount, approve, dispense)

feedback.text: PA needs approve, whose guard amount <= 100 is false at 120; PA cannot run.

answer.text: Path PE (enterAmount, approve, recheck, approve, dispense)

feedback.text: PE also starts with approve (amount <= 100), which fails at 120.

answer.text: No feasible path — 120 blocks every route

feedback.text: 120 satisfies decline (amount >= 101), so PB runs; 120 is a valid witness for PB.

generalfeedback.text: At amount = 120, approve (amount <= 100) is disabled but decline (amount >= 101) is enabled, so from Checking the machine takes decline to Denied, then eject to Idle — path PB. 120 is a valid PB witness (the solver's smallest is 101).

questiontext.text: The app notes that judging a path feasible is "exactly a path-condition satisfiability check." Which analysis does this correspond to?

answer.text: Symbolic execution — collect the path condition (conjunction of guards) and ask a solver whether it is satisfiable

feedback.text: Correct — path feasibility is the satisfiability of the accumulated path condition, the core of symbolic execution.

answer.text: Random testing — throw inputs until one happens to fit

feedback.text: The app uses a constraint solver on the guard conjunction, not blind random search.

answer.text: State coverage — visiting every state at least once

feedback.text: State coverage counts visited states; feasibility is about satisfying the path's guards.

answer.text: Mutation testing — seeding faults to score a suite

feedback.text: Mutation testing is unrelated; feasibility is a satisfiability check on the path condition.

generalfeedback.text: Each guard along a path contributes a clause to the path condition. Deciding feasibility is deciding whether that conjunction is satisfiable and, if so, producing a witness — precisely what symbolic execution does.

questiontext.text: The app links a guard to logic coverage: "a guard is a predicate, and clause binding solves it the same way." What is meant?

answer.text: A guard is a boolean predicate over amount, and finding an amount that makes it true is the same as binding a logic clause to a concrete value

feedback.text: Correct — solving a guard for a satisfying input is the same solver task as binding a logic-coverage clause.

answer.text: A guard must always be false for coverage to succeed

feedback.text: Guards must be satisfiable to yield a test; being false is what makes a branch infeasible.

answer.text: Clause binding replaces guards with states

feedback.text: Clause binding maps a predicate to a concrete input; it does not turn guards into states.

answer.text: A predicate can only be solved by hand, never by a tool

feedback.text: The app's constraint solver binds the predicate automatically to a witness value.

generalfeedback.text: A guard such as amount <= 100 is a predicate over the data. Producing an amount that satisfies the path's predicates is exactly the clause-binding problem in logic coverage — the same constraint solver handles both.

name.text: Infeasible: contradiction, not the states visited

questiontext.text: An abstract path collects the guards amount >= 1, amount <= 100, and amount >= 200. A student says it is infeasible "because it visits the Denied state." Why is that reasoning wrong?

answer.text: Visiting Denied is perfectly legal; the path is infeasible only because amount <= 100 and amount >= 200 cannot both hold

feedback.text: Correct — feasibility is about the guard conjunction, not which states the path passes through.

answer.text: The reasoning is right — reaching Denied always makes a path infeasible

feedback.text: Denied is reachable by feasible paths too (e.g. PB); the real cause is the contradictory guards.

answer.text: Denied has no incoming transitions, so it cannot be visited

feedback.text: Denied does have incoming transitions (decline, fraudHold); the infeasibility is the guard contradiction.

answer.text: The path is infeasible because it is too long

feedback.text: Length is irrelevant; amount cannot be both <= 100 and >= 200, which is the true reason.

generalfeedback.text: Denied is visited by feasible paths as well, so passing through it says nothing about feasibility. This path is infeasible strictly because its guard conjunction amount <= 100 and amount >= 200 is unsatisfiable — no single amount satisfies both.
